sections.html:
Simpsonville lies in southeastern Greenville County between Mauldin and Fountain Inn. Interstate 385 passes through with exits 26 to 29, about 14 miles from Greenville, so your house competes with others across the whole Greenville area. The city was incorporated on August 13, 1901, and its population grew from 195 in 1900 to 23,354 in the 2020 census.

A town that grew that fast has homes from several eras, and each era has its own repair profile. Check your deed and plat for restrictions or an association before you list.

The City of Simpsonville issues building permits, runs building inspections and handles zoning. Greenville County issues land disturbance permits. The residential development guide lists these permit types:

  • Building permits for new structures and additions
  • Electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits
  • Grading permits, and in some cases a county land disturbance permit
  • Right-of-way or encroachment permits
  • In-ground swimming pool permits
  • Sewer tap permits

Schedule inspections by calling City Hall at (864) 967-9526. A final inspection produces a certificate. If earlier work on your house was done without permits, a buyer's attorney may raise it, so gather whatever records you have. Ask City Hall about fees and timelines.

Trash and yard waste pickup from Public Works runs Monday through Friday on fixed routes, with holiday weeks pushing pickup back a day. Adding a second trash can costs a one-time $75.

Sewer responsibility splits at the street. The city maintains only the sewer main, usually in the street, and the property owner is responsible for the lateral line from the house to the main. Stormwater on your own lot is also the owner's job. A sewer backup call goes to Public Works at (864) 967-9531 during business hours.

A cracked or root-damaged lateral is the kind of problem that shows up on a buyer's inspection, so know its status before you negotiate.

Your tax bill comes from Greenville County, and January 15 is the date to remember. Because the tax follows the property and not the person, the buyer and seller need to agree on who covers any balance. Bills usually mail around the end of October. After January 15 the penalties stack up like this:

DateWhat happens
January 15Last day to pay without penalty
January 163 percent penalty added
February 2Another 7 percent added
March 17Another 5 percent plus a $15 execution cost

If you are short on time before a sale, ask the county tax office for a payoff figure so the closing attorney can include it on the settlement statement.

The county treats January 1 as its record date, which explains why a bill can show the prior owner for the year of sale. A homeowner may hold the 4 percent legal residence rate by filing an application before January 15.

That rate stays behind. The sale is an assessable transfer of interest, so the county resets value to market as of December 31 of the sale year, and the new owner files a fresh application. Tell the buyer's attorney whether you had the 4 percent rate, so the next bill holds no shock.

South Carolina's disclosure law has most sellers hand over a written property condition statement before the buyer signs. On each subject, which includes structure, plumbing, electrical, heating, termites and environmental hazards, you either report what you know or state that you make no representation.

A number of transfers fall outside the rule: court-ordered sales, sales by a fiduciary administering an estate, and deals where both parties agree in writing to skip the form. A missing form does not void a contract, but knowingly false answers can make a seller answer for the buyer's actual damages. Inheriting the house or serving as trustee? Ask the attorney whether the exemption fits you.

sections.h2: Selling with repairs or paperwork problems
sections.html: Simpsonville sellers often run into a lateral line that needs work, an older roof, missing permit records or an unpaid tax balance. None of these makes a house unsellable, but each changes who your buyer will be. Someone using a loan will ask for repairs and credits. A cash buyer accepts the house as it stands and adjusts the price instead. Choosing between them is easier when you know the cost of each problem.

Put the buyer's own funds where a lender would be, and nothing waits on an appraisal or loan approval. The attorney, the title search and the deed filing at the county all stay in place, and South Carolina's statute expressly permits an as-is sale.

Your decision tends to rest on three figures: the amount you owe, the repair bill if you listed and the number of months you can keep paying for the house. Ask for any offer in writing, learn the closing date and have the attorney explain every line of the settlement statement before you sign.

Listing is the other path. It means showings, an inspection and the risk that a lender's appraisal lands under the contract price. Either route is reasonable, so pick the one that matches your schedule and repair budget.

sections.h2: From first call to closing day
sections.html:
Expect a brief talk about the house first: how old it is, what is worn out and whether someone lives in it. We look at the property in its present state, then mail an offer if one makes sense. Weigh it against the time and expense of a listing.

Agree, and a closing date gets set. The attorney runs the title search, checks with the county on taxes and with the city on open permits or code matters, and drafts the deed. At the closing you sign, your mortgage and any tax balance come out of the proceeds and the deed goes on record with Greenville County.

On the way out, cancel or transfer utility accounts and ask City Hall to confirm nothing remains open on the address.

Bring your newest Greenville County tax bill, a mortgage payoff figure, permit records and any notices from the city. A rental house also needs the lease. With those items in hand, a buyer can move from interest to a firm offer without a long round of questions.

Also decide ahead of time who will sign. If more than one person owns the house, or an estate holds it, every required signer should be lined up before a closing date is promised.

faqs.q: Which office issues building permits in Simpsonville?
faqs.a: The City of Simpsonville does. It handles building permits, building inspections and zoning, while Greenville County issues land disturbance permits. City Hall is reachable at (864) 967-9526.

faqs.q: When are Greenville County property taxes due for a Simpsonville house?
faqs.a: Pay by January 15 to avoid penalties. The first, 3 percent, begins January 16, and more follow on February 2 and March 17. Bills generally go out toward the end of October.

faqs.q: Does the buyer or the seller pay the property tax when a Simpsonville house sells?
faqs.a: The tax follows the property rather than the person, so the two sides must agree. The closing statement is where that usually gets settled, and your closing attorney can show how the year is split.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for the sewer line on a Simpsonville property?
faqs.a: The city maintains the main in the street, and the owner is responsible for the lateral from the house to that main. Sewer problems during business hours go to Public Works at (864) 967-9531.

faqs.q: Do I need to disclose problems with my Simpsonville house?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The law calls for a written statement unless your sale is exempt. You can share what you know or make no representation, but answers you know are false or misleading can leave you liable.
